<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion, but B consistently converted A's own material into support for its side. Three turns did the damage: (1) B took A's concession that independent central banks are "democratically created and bounded" and reframed it as democracies' highest use of legitimacy being self-binding to competence; (2) B caught the tension in A's "who decides what counts as delivery" move, showing it undercuts A's own error-correction argument, which A never fully repaired; (3) B's pressure question extracted an explicit concession — a fully authorized policy that raises child mortality is still a bad decision — and B crystallized that in closing as proof that authorization is not what makes a public decision good. B also turned A's Ulysses image against him ("the story is about why the sailor must not be obeyed"), and the recurring meta-frame that every virtue A claimed (compliance, durability, correction) is itself an outcome, so results are the master criterion, was a genuinely load-bearing comparison. A's means/ends line — competence governs instruments, the demos chooses ends — remained live and was elegantly delivered in the closing surgeon reversal, and A rightly resisted the Venezuela/Argentina examples as authoritarian rather than democratic failure. But B answered the means/ends split ("ends-setting is competence-dependent all the way down") and pressed the charge that A had drifted toward "legitimacy is the ultimate constitutional source," a claim B never disputed and which is not the motion. A's opening was also clipped for exceeding the cap, a small execution cost. Clear but competitive win for B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's handling of [A2.6]: A offered "central banks are democratically created and bounded" as proof that competence is rented; B flipped it into the claim that a democracy's most considered act is to place being-right beyond the reach of authorization — then re-turned A's own Ulysses rescue by noting the mast is only rational because the rope is right and the sovereign will is wrong at the decisive moment.</best_rebuttal>
